articles.title: How to keep your Mac awake, even when your MacBook lid is closed
articles.subtitle: macOS is designed to put your Mac to sleep when it is not being used. That is usually exactly what you want. Sleep saves power, protects battery life, and keeps a MacBook from running when it is closed and stuffed in a bag.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
macOS is designed to put your Mac to sleep when it is not being used. That is usually exactly what you want. Sleep saves power, protects battery life, and keeps a MacBook from running when it is closed and stuffed in a bag.

Sometimes tasks like downloads, backups, remote sessions, and AI coding need a temporary exception. Fortunately, there are some great Mac apps for giving you this control.

Limited solutions that are included with macOS

Apple gives you some control in System Settings.

On macOS, you can go to System Settings > Lock Screen to change when the display turns off, and on Mac laptops you can use System Settings > Battery > Options to prevent automatic sleeping on the power adapter when the display is off.

Apple also supports using a Mac laptop with the lid closed when it is connected to power and paired with an external display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad.

I generally prefer not to make those settings permanent. Most of the time, I want my Mac to sleep normally. What I want instead is a quick, intentional override that I can turn on for a specific job and turn off when I am done.

For that, there are three Mac utilities worth knowing.

KeepingYouAwake is the simple one-click toggle

KeepingYouAwake is the utility that has lived in my Mac menu bar the longest.

It is free, lightweight, and built around the same basic idea that made Caffeine popular years ago: click a menu bar icon, and your Mac stays awake. Click it again, and your Mac returns to its normal sleep behavior.

I started using KeepingYouAwake years ago when Macs moved to Retina displays. Caffeine, the classic coffee-cup utility, did not make that transition to high-resolution design.

KeepingYouAwake became the simple replacement. It honors the spirit of Caffeine with no dashboard or complex automation. It’s just a reliable on/off switch for the Mac’s default sleep behavior.

You can activate it indefinitely or for preset durations, and it can automatically disable itself when your MacBook battery drops below a set level. It supports Retina displays and Dark Mode, and under the hood it uses Apple’s built-in caffeinate command-line utility.

The important limitation: KeepingYouAwake is not the closed-lid solution. Its own documentation is clear that, because of macOS limitations and thermal considerations, it only prevents sleep on desktop Macs and portable Macs with the lid open.

That makes KeepingYouAwake ideal for the simple stuff: reading, presentations, screen recordings, long downloads, or any time you are still using the Mac and just do not want the screen or system to nod off. It is the utility I use as my everyday “do not sleep yet” toggle.

Amphetamine is the gold standard for closed-lid sessions

When I actually want to close my MacBook and keep a task running, Amphetamine is the app I open.

Following Microsoft's mass layoffs, The Elder Scrolls Online has ended up in a transitional period while remaining staff work to forge a path forwards. If you want evidence of effects the cuts are already starting to have on the MMO, look no further than its Crown Store.

ESO's version of the premium currency cash shop that's become a hallmark of most massive online games with stuff to hawk - for real money, in-game money, or either depending on how much time you want to spend grinding - is undergoing some changes following the cuts.

"To help manage workload, we have decided to remove the Web Crown Store from the official elderscrollsonline. com website on Wednesday, July 22nd," ZeniMax community manager Kevin Gbolie wrote in an update on the game's forums yesterday, spotted by PC Gamer.

"The ability to acquire crowns via the website will remain and, of course, this does not affect the items that will be offered on the Crown Store in The Elder Scrolls Online, you will just need to login into the game to view and purchase the latest offerings. Furthermore, for the same reason, the monthly Crown Store Showcase blog will also change. "

So, you'll still be able to buy virtual cash via the game's website, but to browse the store you'll need to boot up the game. Gbolie noted that the blog changes are "due to team bandwidth", and will see these rundowns of new stuff players can buy become "more list-like than anything else".

Aside from the obvious impact on people buying the outfits, furnishings, mounts, and more sold via the store, the web version's demise will also have consequences for the MMO's pages on the Unofficial Elder Scrolls Pages (UESP) wiki, who are losing easy access to high resolution official screenshots they currently lean on. "The goal is to provide what we can," Gbolie added in a comment.

"Especially because we know folks like UESP do use those shots. But to be blunt, the team responsible for the blog and those screenshots doesn't have the capacity to provide those at the scale we could before. But we will provide what we can for now and adjust from there. "

Given ESO's likely in a position following the mass cuts where demonstrating that the game can keep on being a valuable source of cash for ZeniMax and Microsoft by extension is paramount, I can only imagine how its remaining developers are feeling as they struggle to hold up the roof on an aspect of ESO which is key to that.

My thinking is, if there aren't enough hands left to keep the store running as it was, what sorts of cuts might bits of the game not as tangibly linked to keeping the lights on suffer in the future?

articles.title: I’m a die-hard Apple user. Here’s the travel tech I refuse to leave at home
articles.subtitle: Macworld One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives). We try to go on an international trip every 18 months or so.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives). We try to go on an international trip every 18 months or so. Our most recent trip abroad was to South Africa in 2024, and we’re heading to Iceland this August. Then there are weekends away a few times a year.

Every great trip requires planning, whether it’s an overnight stay an hour away from home or a grand vacation in a country I’ve never visited before. Besides all the travel logistics (that my wife handles), there’s the tech you need to bring, which is my responsibility in my household.

Over the years, I’ve figured out what tech I absolutely need to take with me. There’s an art to figuring out what to bring. You don’t want to overdo it, because you’ll end up lugging around stuff you aren’t using. But you don’t want to be left without that thing you absolutely need and don’t really have a means of obtaining that item where you are.

While I now rely on my iPhone for all the photos and videos I shoot, I need other items to ensure a successful and enjoyable trip. Here’s a list of the gear I bring with me on my trips. This is the stuff I almost always bring no matter where I’m going. Hopefully, you can use this list to help you figure out what you need to bring on your next trip. If you have suggestions, drop me a line at rloyola@macworld.com. (Note: Prices stated here are MSRPs, but Amazon often runs sales and discounts on many of them.)

iPhone 17 Pro Max

Britta O’Boyle

There was a time when I would bring separate video and still cameras on every trip, but the iPhone has gotten so good, I don’t need any other camera. With some practice and knowledge of iOS’s features and settings, or with third-party camera apps, you can replicate the capabilities of cameras that cost hundreds more. Before the iPhone 17 Pro Max, I used an iPhone 16 Plus, but I really prefer to the Pro’s telephoto lens.

MacBook Neo

Eugen Wegmann

On longer trips where I’ll shoot a lot of photos and video, I bring a MacBook so I can browse and manage my shots after each day is done. I used to bring an extremely old MacBook Pro instead of the MacBook Pro that I use daily, so if it was lost, stolen, or damaged on the trip, I wouldn’t sweat it that much. But it’s also extremely slow and heavy.

Even with a recent $100 price hike, the MacBook Neo is such a delight–lightweight, fast, and durable. And as I point out in my review, it doesn’t need to be a secondary machine—the Neo is extremely capable of being a daily-use Mac.

Saily for international eSIMs

Foundry

My carrier offers international connectivity by partnering with carriers in other countries. I’ve mostly had success with it, but sometimes there are gaps in coverage or the speeds are slow. On my last trip abroad, I tried a different approach: I took advantage of the iPhone’s dual eSIM and used Saily to get a second native eSIM in the country I was visiting.

With a second eSIM, I was able to switch between it and my carrier’s offering to get the best possible connection. Overseas eSIMs are affordable–sometimes they’re really cheap, making it worth a try. Learn more about using an eSIM when traveling and about using two eSIMs in an iPhone.

Anker Nano Travel Adapter

Foundry

More and more hotels, especially those that cater to international clientele, are starting to install wall outlets that can be used with the different types of power plugs. Hotels are also starting to have USB charging ports next to those wall outlets. But they’re not everywhere, so when you travel outside of the country, it’s good to have a power outlet adapter. The $26 Anker Nano Travel Adapter works in over 200 countries (it is not a voltage converter), and it can charge five devices at once.

articles.title: WhatCable gives you the download on your USB cables
articles.subtitle: If you’ve ever wondered why your data transfers to external drives aren’t going as fast as you’d like, or a certain peripheral just isn’t working, you could probably use WhatCable, a helpful little app from developer Darryl Morley.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
If you’ve ever wondered why your data transfers to external drives aren’t going as fast as you’d like, or a certain peripheral just isn’t working, you could probably use WhatCable, a helpful little app from developer Darryl Morley.

WhatCable looks at your Mac’s USB ports and anything plugged into them, and lets you know about speeds and power supply for your currently connected USB and Thunderbolt cables, as well as what their maximums are. While there are other places on your Mac that you can find this information, such as System Information, WhatCable presents it all in a well organized, easy to read manner. It even details all the devices connected to your USB hubs.

For example, after looking at it, I realized that my backup drive was only connected via a USB2 cable. Fine in general for overnight backups, but when it reminded to me when I was troubleshooting some backup issues that maybe I should switch to a high speed cable that supports USB-3. 1

You can choose to run WhatCable in your menu bar, or as a standalone app; there’s also a “Show technical details” option that gives you even more information that could be helpful for troubleshooting. There are options for font size, translucency, and menu bar icon, in case you’re so inclined.

For its base functionality, WhatCable is free and available either via Morley’s site, or via homebrew. For a £9.99 one-time purchase, you can unlock WhatCable Pro, which works on up to two Macs, lets you assign names to cables so you can remember which one it is when you plug it in later, provides more in-depth diagnostics, offers live power metering to see how much juice is being delivered right now, and even more.

[via Michael Tsai ]

Holy cow did that backup go way faster. ↩

articles.title: The better way to use Gemini on the Mac
articles.subtitle: Back in April, Google joined OpenAI and Anthropic in offering a dedicated Mac app for its AI chatbot software. Two months later, it’s clear that Gemini for Mac isn’t as good as it could be.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Back in April, Google joined OpenAI and Anthropic in offering a dedicated Mac app for its AI chatbot software. Two months later, it’s clear that Gemini for Mac isn’t as good as it could be.

Gemini for Mac isn’t a very good macOS app

Because I’m interested in AI technology and its progression over time, I’ve used Gemini on my Mac regularly since before the Mac app was rumored.

I’m also a Safari user. For that reason, my solution to using Gemini on the Mac has been Safari’s “Add to Dock” feature.

When Gemini first arrived on the Mac as a dedicated app, I still preferred my Safari “Add to Dock” instance. I just like that Command + N opens a new chat window, and I can have many open chat windows.

This way of multitasking is better for me than switching between conversation threads. I’m more likely to forget about a task in a chat thread if it’s not an open window on my Mac.

Missing features and app icon jail

I also have at least one chat thread that doesn’t actually work on Gemini’s Mac app. It works fine in the Safari “Add to Dock” version, though, since that’s just the website presented as an app.

Instead of letting me continue the chat, Gemini’s Mac app replaces the text entry box with a button to open the website. I’d rather just use my Safari web app version where it works fine.

The use of the word “yet” in the message is doing a lot of work at this point.

Another complaint is the icon. Gemini’s Mac app is in icon jail.

Icon jail is a dumb Apple behavior for app icons on macOS Tahoe that aren’t drawn in the exact shape and size that Apple forces.

While that’s an Apple-forced problem for Mac apps that predate Apple’s dumb rule, the Gemini Mac app arrived months after macOS Tahoe was released.

Then there’s the thing that prompted me to mention how I’m using Gemini on my Mac in the first place.

This week on Daring Fireball, John Gruber wrote about why he uninstalled the Gemini Mac app:

The thing that really turns me off about the Gemini Mac app is Google’s gall. The Gemini app installs a background helper named “GeminiAppLauncher” in your login items. It also installs “GoogleUpdater” as a process with the privilege to launch in the background whenever it wants. Gemini never asks for permission to install either of these, and, most arrogantly, if you, as an informed user, remove either of them, the Gemini app silently adds them back. There is no setting in Gemini to disable this.

This made me realize that I’ve literally kept the Gemini Mac app around just to check for app updates. While there are occasional updates, they haven’t fixed my two issues with the software yet.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

articles.title: Xbox Backward Compatibility Is Coming To PC Starting With Conker: Live And Reloaded
articles.subtitle: Backwards Compatability Conker PC Xbox Xbox announced today that some original Xbox games, including Conker: Live and Reloaded, will be fully playable on PC via its digital store. These OG Xbox games will include new visual settings and features.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Backwards Compatability Conker PC Xbox

Xbox announced today that some original Xbox games, including Conker: Live and Reloaded, will be fully playable on PC via its digital store. These OG Xbox games will include new visual settings and features. And eventually, Xbox plans to add achievements to these older titles, too.

On July 22, Xbox confirmed that four original Xbox games will be made available to buy and play on the Xbox PC app. These games are BLiNX: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Bill Gates’ favorite video game, Fuzion Frenzy. It’s an interesting selection made up of Xbox exclusives and launch titles for the 2001 console.

Xbox says that to start playing these games on PC, you just have to boot up the Xbox app on PC, buy one of them, and start playing. If you already own the game on console, you don’t need to buy it again.

However, according to Xbox’s minimum specs, it appears your PC must be running Windows 11. I’m still on Windows 10 and can’t currently see these games on the Xbox app. Boo.

“Your library is more than just a collection of games,” said Jason Ronald, VP of next generation (stop giggling) at Xbox. “It is your personal history of epic stories and treasured memories from the past. And as players, we don’t want to leave our gaming legacy behind even as technology continues to evolve and advance. We expect our library of games to move forward with us and to be able to play them in entirely new ways.”

Xbox says these PC versions will feature new visual options, including 4x resolution upscaling, VSync support, fullscreen and windowed modes, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, “and more.”

And in the near future, Xbox says it will begin to add achievements to “select” original Xbox games on both PC and console. These first four games will get achievements in “the coming months.”

“This marks the beginning of a broader effort to preserve XBOX games from the past and bring them to PC over time,” said Ronald. I hope more original Xbox and Xbox 360 games get backward compatibility support across console and PC. And I hope Sony and Nintendo are paying attention and maybe follow in Xbox’s footsteps, because it is wild to me that Xbox is still doing a better job at making old games easily accessible and playable than either of those other gaming giants.

articles.title: Lil Finder Guy pet was the gateway to building my own Mac apps with Codex
articles.subtitle: At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet. This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it?
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet.

This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it? My first real task with Codex was putting together a virtual Lil Finder Guy for fun.

A month later, I’m using two Mac apps that Codex built at my direction. Toying around with Codex Pets was the gateway for me to better understand its capabilities.

OpenAI tools for making apps have improved a lot since last summer

Both Mac apps are just for my use and not intended for distribution, but that’s just a choice and not a Codex limitation. They’re genuinely usable and useful software applications that serve my needs.

One tool is called Flow, and it just helps me track activity and changes around the App Store. Another offers a better experience with using a social network on the Mac without certain constraints of Chrome, like minimum window width.

The experience taught me just how much these tools have changed since this time last year as well.

For example, I wanted to make my own Launchpad replacement when macOS Tahoe removed the feature from the Mac last June. (Launchpad wasn’t for everyone, but it was part of my muscle memory since OS X Lion. I’ve since moved on from missing it.)

Using ChatGPT to walk me through Xcode while copying and pasting blocks of code and screenshots of errors was a process void of much joy. Even as a proof-of-concept, I couldn’t get the app that I was making to resemble the behavior that I had in mind. Nuking the project felt good.

With Codex, I had a functioning app that solved my specific need in almost no time (and literally no Xcode). I was able to go from idea to minimum viable software almost immediately. The rest of my first month with Codex and making the app was spent adding features beyond my original need and getting more specific about how things should look and behave.

There are more tools that I want to make for myself next, and having Codex’s capabilities on the Mac has been a real boost.

(Next, I’ll be watching Apple’s WWDC announcements with a new eye for what additional capabilities become available. I’m also cautious about any changes that may break my newfound system for turning ideas into functioning tools.)

Computer Use in Codex is a major unlock

Part of what makes Codex good at this compared to my experience using ChatGPT a year ago is that the model and app are made for coding and generally just doing things for you.

ChatGPT will absorb most or all of this functionality as a feature within the main app, but the extent of this remains to be seen. For now, there’s one thing in particular about Codex that made all the difference in the world: Computer Use.

Codex is far from the only coding agent available on the Mac, and it’s not the only version with a computer use feature either. But Codex’s Computer Use feature is phenomenal. On the Mac, it works in the background without taking over your machine. For me, this has meant I’ve been able to use my Mac, uninterrupted, while this coding agent expertly follows my direction.

Codex’s Computer Use essentially unlocks the complete opposite experience from what ChatGPT provided in this department last summer. Instead of it providing me with guidance and not much perspective, I’ve been able to guide it and vastly expand my own perspective.

articles.title: Redditors’ Fake Duskbloods Boss Guides Fool Google’s Dumbass Delusion Machine
articles.subtitle: AI Dawn-Eater Abomination FromSoftware The Duskbloods Reddit users, bored waiting for more information about the forthcoming FromSoftware Switch 2 exclusive The Duskbloods, have just been making up details about it for themselves.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
AI Dawn-Eater Abomination FromSoftware The Duskbloods

Reddit users, bored waiting for more information about the forthcoming FromSoftware Switch 2 exclusive The Duskbloods, have just been making up details about it for themselves.

As reported by Ian Walker (I recognize that name from somewhere ) over on Video Game Town, this “Duskposting”—where users make up imaginary bosses from the game, detail them, and even write guides for how to beat them—has been popular since the game’s announcement.

It’s all good harmless fun, right up until the LLMs mindlessly scrape the made-up information and then present it to the rest of the world as stone-cold fact.

One of the most fundamental flaws of LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok is their vulnerabilities to bullshit. Being fancy predictive text engines with no actual intelligence at all, such so-called “AI” isn’t capable of genuine understanding or comprehension, and doesn’t actually know anything. This is incredibly easily exploited, by seeding the internet the LLMs are scraping with nonsense information on specific subjects, which will then be regurgitated with absolutely confidence by the chatbots.

This phenomenon was rather splendidly demonstrated by BBC reporter Thomas Germain earlier this year, when he wrote a completely fictional article on his personal blog detailing which tech journalists were best at hot dog-eating competitions.

Naturally ranking himself first, he detailed how he and many of his peers had taken part in a competitive eating event that doesn’t exist, and within 24 hours this information was being spat out as fact by Gemini and ChatGPT, which had pulled it from a single, relatively little-read source.

Now, given the complete absence of any legitimate information regarding The Duskbloods —which finally receives its first network test in August —Redditors are discovering they have had exactly the same effect. For instance, just this moment I typed into Google, “Which bosses are hardest to beat in The Duskbloods?” and before any actual search results appeared, Gemini stepped in to answer the question:

The hardest bosses in The Duskbloods include Lycan Vrykolakas, Dawn-Eater Abomination, and Jocasta, Eminence of the Night.

It doesn’t stop there, though. It then provides me with a text header reading “Hardest Boss Breakdown,” and then, as LLMs love to do, gives me a bullet-pointed list of the three aforementioned adversaries and why they’re considered the toughest. For Dawn-Eater Abomination, for instance, it says,

Notorious for its frustrating multiplying mechanics, small mob spawns, and cramped arena space in the Stygian Citadel, making solo attempts a severe headache.

To be abundantly clear, FromSoftware has announced no information at all about anything in The Duskbloods, least of all the boss names, and we naturally have no idea yet just what level of headache they might provide. Gemini (which at least very clearly links to citations) has only one source for every single one of these replies, and that’s r/TheDuskbloods. Gemini then kindly concludes,

Ignore the Backrow: Leave distant ranged spawns alone and prioritize the fast-moving melee mobs rushing your position. Burst the Core: Damage the boss only when all small mobs are dead to advance the phase quickly. Claude Code for desktop now works with Apple’s iOS Simulator, giving developers a direct way to build, launch, and test iPhone apps inside the Mac app. Anthropic has released the integration in public beta for supported users.

The new feature adds an interactive simulator pane beside the Claude Code conversation. Developers can ask Claude to build an app, run it in the simulator, check a specific screen, or test a user flow while watching the process live.

Set us as a preferred source and our Apple reporting ranks higher in your Google Search results and Discover feed — one tap, no account changes.

Claude can install the app, interact with buttons and menus, read what appears on the screen, and make changes based on what it finds. Developers can also use taps and swipes inside the simulator while Claude continues working.

How the iOS Simulator Integration Works

Claude Code on desktop now works with the iOS simulator. Build and run your iOS app, and the simulator opens in a panel right next to your conversation. Available today in public beta. pic.twitter.com/su4IguzPVb — ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) July 21, 2026

Claude Code on desktop now works with the iOS simulator. Build and run your iOS app, and the simulator opens in a panel right next to your conversation. Available today in public beta. pic.twitter.com/su4IguzPVb

To use the feature, developers need Claude Code Desktop on macOS, along with Xcode and the iOS platform installed. The integration works with projects that can build an app for the iOS Simulator.

Users can open the Code tab, choose the app project as the project folder, and ask Claude to run or test the app. For example, a developer can ask Claude to build the app and check the onboarding flow.

When the app launches, the simulator pane opens beside the conversation. Claude then uses the simulator directly, which means it does not need macOS Accessibility or Screen Recording permissions for this workflow.

The feature works only in local sessions because cloud and SSH sessions cannot access the simulators installed on a user’s Mac. Anthropic also says the integration remains limited to macOS because Apple’s iOS Simulator does not run on Windows or Linux.

Claude Code sends screenshots from the simulator to Anthropic and stores them under the company’s standard conversation retention settings. Anthropic advises developers not to sign in to real accounts on any simulated device that Claude uses.

The iOS Simulator integration is available in Claude Desktop version 1.24012.0 or later for Pro, Max, and Team users during the public beta.
